messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Margaret is a 73-year-old painter who lives alone in the home she once shared with her husband. Two years ago, a man-made disaster took his life and shattered her world. It was a fire at the community arts center where she had her studio. Her husband had come to see her new series. A man who had been drinking heavily knocked over a kerosene heater; the smell of alcohol saturated the room. In the chaos, someone pushed Margaret from behind, hands on her shoulders, and she stumbled out. She turned back, but it was too late. Her husband did not make it. She remembers the scene in photographic detail—the orange glow, his face, the heat on her skin. When the memory comes, she feels her body lock in that same position, frozen and helpless, and a wave of guilt crashes over her: she should have pulled him out, she should have died instead. She has come to believe that her life is no longer worth living, that she will never feel normal emotions again, and that her previous trust in the world has been completely destroyed.

In the months after, every-day life became a minefield. The smell of alcohol coming from a neighbor’s breath instantly drops her back into that burning room, her body stiffening. The same happens when someone touches her unexpectedly—a pat on the back, a hand on her arm—she startles and feels her skin crawl. She becomes irritable, snapping at anyone who comes too close, and she finds herself listening for sounds that might mean someone is entering her home. Because she believes she is fundamentally broken and that the world is unsafe, she is hypervigilant, checking locks multiple times a night. That same belief makes her sensitive to crying; the sight of a tearful face on television reminds her of her own emotional deadness, and she turns away. Her conviction that she will never recover also distorts how she remembers the event: the memory feels even more like a photographic slide, alien and fixed, because she cannot imagine ever feeling differently. The guilt that clings to the memory makes her scan every room for the scent of alcohol, so she now notices that smell from a distance. And when the memory intrudes, her irritability spikes and she lies awake, convinced that someone is outside. The memory also deepens her guilt and reinforces her belief that she is worthless. The constant irritability and the nightly hypervigilance wear her down, and she finds more evidence that her life is not worth living.

Margaret avoids news reports about fires. She tries hard not to think about the event. She keeps her mind occupied by painting for hours every day, filling canvases with tranquil landscapes, but the work is mechanical, without the emotion she once had. She no longer attends gallery openings. The last time she did, a friend touched her elbow in encouragement, and Margaret had to leave in tears. That moment, a few weeks ago, finally convinced her to seek help. She is most afraid that she will never feel anything except guilt, but she hopes that talking about it might quiet the photographs in her mind.

violation_explanations: No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory directly influences or leads to triggers; the vignette shows memory leading to guilt (appraisals) which then increases sensitivity to triggers, but not a direct memory-to-triggers causal relationship.
